For the school science fair, Kavya wanted to answer a question that had bothered her for weeks: do plants grow better with music? Her uncle said that his tomatoes grew faster when the radio was on. Her brother said that was nonsense. Kavya decided to find out properly.

She took six small pots, filled each with the same soil, and planted three bean seeds in each. Three pots went in her bedroom, where she played music for two hours every evening. The other three went in the kitchen, where it was quiet. She gave every pot the same cup of water each morning and wrote everything in a notebook: the date, the time, and the height of every shoot, measured with a ruler. "A fair test," her teacher had said, "changes only one thing."

Every year, between January and March, olive ridley turtles come ashore on the beach near Sanjay's village to lay their eggs. They come at night, in hundreds, and dig holes in the sand with their back flippers. Each turtle lays about a hundred eggs, covers them, and returns to the sea. She never sees her young.

When Sanjay was small, people took the eggs to eat or to sell, and dogs dug up the rest. Fewer turtles came each year. Then a group of fishermen, including Sanjay's father, started a hatchery: a fenced square of sand where eggs could be moved and kept safe. This year, for the first time, Sanjay was allowed to join the night patrol. He was twelve, and he had been waiting for this since he was eight.

He had no running shoes. On the morning of the race he ran barefoot, in a white vest his mother had sewn the night before. The ants did not come back. At dinner, her mother announced that the case was closed, and Varun asked for an apology, which he received, along with a small spoon of sugar.
